impact_innovation.extended_summary: When an employee at John's Pharmacy told owner Abe Funk she'd probably have to quit after her second baby, he went home and told his wife: 'We're going to open a daycare.' The Cape Girardeau pharmacy opened one in 2023, and it's helped him keep and attract staff ever since. 'It's like any other benefit, like a 401(k) or healthcare,' Funk said. 'If we didn't have staff, we couldn't stay open.' Now Missouri's Child Care Works program is adding state money on top of what employers already provide, and $1.46 million in federal Rural Health Transformation funding will expand childcare support for rural healthcare employers statewide.

impact_innovation.title: Virginia Beach wastewater facility to turn biogas into power for thousands of homes
impact_innovation.summary: A Virginia Beach wastewater plant will soon turn flushed biogas into renewable natural gas — enough to power 5,000 homes a year. Instead of flaring off methane, the new system purifies it and feeds it into the local gas pipeline.
impact_innovation.extended_summary: The flush of a toilet could soon help power homes across Hampton Roads. Right now, the Hampton Roads Sanitation District burns off the methane that bubbles up during wastewater treatment — flaring it into the sky. A new $30 million facility will instead purify that biogas and funnel it through a 200-foot interconnection pipe into Virginia Natural Gas lines, producing enough renewable gas to power 5,000 homes annually. 'There's an environmental benefit to this in that we are pretty much eliminating that flared gas,' said Carl Garofalo of Southern Company Gas. It's a byproduct of wastewater treatment turned into a regional energy resource.

impact_innovation.title: Want the News to Unite People? Let Them Report It
impact_innovation.summary: In Akron, Ohio, hundreds of regular residents are stepping up to cover school board and city meetings through a program called Documenters. Their write-ups create a public record of local decisions, helping people feel more connected and empowered in their community.
impact_innovation.extended_summary: Jackie Jantzi isn't a professional reporter, but every few weeks she sits in on Akron school board meetings, takes notes, and publishes a summary for anyone to read. She's one of hundreds of residents working with local news outlet Signal Akron through a program called Documenters. These citizen write-ups let a tiny newsroom cover way more ground and give residents a real-time record of the decisions shaping their lives. As local news shrinks nationwide, this grassroots approach is rebuilding trust and civic power from the ground up.

impact_innovation.title: A runway success
impact_innovation.summary: After a storm ripped a massive hole in its roof, the Tillamook Air Museum was saved by a Utah nonprofit that purchased the hangar for $1 and repaired it. The museum is now set for a grand reopening.
impact_innovation.extended_summary: When a December storm tore a 6,000-square-foot hole in the roof of the Tillamook Air Museum's historic Hangar B, the future looked bleak. Repair costs reached millions, and the museum closed indefinitely. Then the Utah-based Vintage Aviation Museum stepped in, purchasing the hangar for just $1 and committing to repairs. Ten months later, the museum is ready for a grand reopening. The rescue not only saves a piece of WWII history—Hangar B is one of the largest wooden structures in the world—but also preserves a community landmark.

impact_innovation.title: After nearly a decade, feds find home for Mississippi dredge sand
impact_innovation.summary: After nearly a decade of searching, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has finally found a home for dredge sand from the Mississippi River—a new city port in Wabasha, Minnesota. The solution avoids burying a family farm and ends years of community pushback.
impact_innovation.extended_summary: For nearly ten years, towering mounds of dredge sand sat along the Mississippi River near Wabasha, Minnesota—a temporary fix with no permanent home. The Army Corps had once planned to dump it on a fourth-generation family farm, a move that sparked community backlash and eminent domain fights. This month, crews finally started moving the sand to a new $4.6 million city port and terminal, where it'll be stored or reused. The arrangement ends a decade-long saga and shows how local pushback and creative problem-solving can lead to a win for everyone.

impact_innovation.title: After wrestling with long COVID, a Brookline writer hopes her card game will help others talk about chronic illness
impact_innovation.summary: After her own long COVID battle, a Brookline writer turned her struggle into SPIKE! — a card game that helps people with chronic illness tell their stories. Players pick images representing their past, present, and future, opening up conversations that are hard to start.
impact_innovation.extended_summary: Denise Brodey knows how isolating chronic illness can feel — so she built a card game to break the silence. SPIKE!, named after the COVID spike protein, uses 27 evocative images (a pink macaroon, a pile of dirty dishes, a stop sign) to help players map their life before illness, their present, and their hopes for the future. Developed as a Harvard Medical School capstone, the game is already being tested with peer support groups and is free to download. Brodey's goal: give patients the language to advocate for themselves in a system where doctors rarely have time to listen.
